tecnicas.observacao: Pacote multiagente e multirrodada: o mesmo LLM atua como TaskLLM (gera o código de planejamento, com análise textual em CoT, Fig. 2), SteerLLM (gera instruções de orientação e decide finalizar) e CheckLLM (gera e executa código de verificação); a análise de um script baseado em regras (Symbolic Complexity Checker) também é devolvida ao SteerLLM, o que o dicionário classifica como feedback de analisador. O prompt de entrada inclui o formato de resposta exigido (<Required Answer Format>, Fig. 2), comum a todas as condições, por isso `restricoes` também está nos comparadores. Base identificável: Code Answer, pois o estudo afirma que com uma só rodada o método funciona identicamente ao Code Answer (PDF p. 5); daí os acrescentados multiagente e feedback. O contrafactual (contra Only Question, Code Answer e demais linhas de base, mesmo LLM e mesmas tarefas) é do pacote completo; o ganho não pode ser atribuído a um mecanismo isolado. Máximo de 3 rodadas de reorientação e regeneração.

citacoes.trecho: Unlike prior work that uses code to interface with robot action modules or pre-designed planners, we steer LLMs to generate code as solvers, planners, and checkers for TAMP tasks requiring symbolic computing, while still leveraging textual reasoning to incorporate common sense.
To address this, we design a multi-agent, multi-round framework with self-checking modules.

We prompt the same LLM to act as three agents: TaskLLM, which generates complete planning code; SteerLLM, which provides guidance prompts to TaskLLM and decides when to finalize the plan; and CheckLLM, which produces checking code to evaluate the correctness of TaskLLM’s output.
Additionally, we introduce a rule-based Symbolic Complexity Checker to analyze the symbolic computation level in the generated code, with its analysis also fed back to SteerLLM.
We set the maximum number of re-guidance and regeneration rounds to 3, after which the final answer is forced to be accepted.
CheckLLM generates and executes code that verifies the correctness of the current answer.

Solve the following question using your coding skills. Suggest python code (in a python coding block) for the user to execute. You can first output your thinking steps with texts and then the final python code.
[Input Question] <Task Explanation> <Environment State> <Required Answer Format>

citacoes.trecho: Code Answer Prompting LLMs to first analyze the question with Chain-of-Thought (COT) [34] and then output the code answer.
The next sub-task is selected from the top K candidates by combining two likelihoods: (1) the LLM-generated likelihood and (2) the feasibility likelihood of each candidate action.
HMAS-2 [25] is a multi-agent framework designed for multi-robot settings, where each robot is equipped with an LLM to provide local feedback to a central LLM planner.
No local feedback is used when applied to single-robot tasks.
For each method, the LLM is prompted with a task description without any few-shot examples.
However, LLMs often produce inconsistent code versions, many of which are ineffective or lack proper symbolic computation.
Generating planners with coding also risks adding errors.
However, in some highly complex cases, the generated code exceeds the 50-second execution time limit, contributing to its performance drop in the most challenging scenarios.

Another major bottleneck we identified is the LLM’s inability to translate real-world application problems into abstract optimization or logistical tasks solvable through code, which is also challenging to human experts.
Third, We also observe that the required output format for plans strongly influences the coding success rate, underscoring the need to enhance LLMs’ self-formalization capabilities for TAMP problems.
When such execution errors occur, we query the three tested methods to re-plan the next steps.
